questions.stem: A grade 3 student whose home language is Wolof enrolls in a New York State school district. Her parents choose an ENL program, and her NYSITELL results place her at the Entering level. Which weekly schedule meets the minimum CR Part 154 requirement for her ENL services?
options: 180 minutes of Stand-alone ENL and 180 minutes of Integrated ENL/ELA
360 minutes of Stand-alone ENL, delivered as daily pull-out sessions
90 minutes of Stand-alone ENL, 180 of Integrated ENL/ELA, and 90 of Integrated ENL/science
180 minutes of Integrated ENL in ELA or in another core content area
questions.why: For grades K–8, CR Part 154 requires an Entering student to receive 360 minutes of ENL per week: 180 minutes of Stand-alone ENL plus 180 minutes of Integrated ENL/ELA. The Stand-alone time builds English with a certified ESOL teacher, and the Integrated ENL/ELA time develops English inside grade-level ELA. Required minutes then decrease as proficiency rises (360, 360, 180, 180, 90).

traps.note: An all pull-out schedule leaves out the required 180 minutes of Integrated ENL/ELA. Part 154 deliberately keeps even Entering students in grade-level ELA with ESOL support instead of separating them full time.
This 360-minute pattern has only 90 Stand-alone minutes, which is the Emerging configuration (with its flexible 90 used as Integrated). Entering students need a full 180 minutes of Stand-alone ENL.
180 minutes of Integrated ENL in ELA or another content area is the Expanding requirement. An Entering student needs twice as many minutes, including Stand-alone ENL.

questions.key: K–8 Entering = 360 min/week: 180 Stand-alone ENL + 180 Integrated ENL/ELA.

questions.stimulus:
Excerpt from a district program guide:
"About half of the students in this program are ELLs whose home language is Spanish, and about half are English-proficient students. All students learn grade-level content in both Spanish and English, and they stay in the program for several years. Our goals are bilingualism, biliteracy, academic achievement, and cross-cultural understanding for every student."
questions.stem: The program described is best identified as which of the following?
options: Transitional Bilingual Education
One-way Dual Language
Two-way Dual Language
Integrated ENL
questions.why: A two-way Dual Language program enrolls both ELLs and English-proficient students and teaches grade-level content in both languages for several years, with bilingualism and biliteracy as goals for every student. A one-way program serves students who are mostly from one language group. TBE also uses two languages, but its goal is to transition ELLs to English-only instruction.

traps.note: TBE also teaches in two languages, but it serves ELLs and aims to move them into English-only instruction. It does not enroll English-proficient students or aim for biliteracy for all.
One-way Dual Language serves students who are mostly from one language group. A program that deliberately mixes ELLs with English-proficient students is two-way.
Integrated ENL is part of an ENL program: content and English development taught in English. It does not teach grade-level content in Spanish or aim for biliteracy.

questions.key: Two-way Dual Language = ELLs + English-proficient peers in two languages, biliteracy for all; one-way = mainly one language group.

questions.stimulus:
Principal's memo:
"To give our grade 1 Entering students their Integrated ENL/ELA minutes, our bilingual paraprofessional will sit with them during the ELA block, which is taught by the classroom teacher. The ESOL teacher will continue to provide their Stand-alone ENL."
questions.stem: Which response to the principal's plan best reflects CR Part 154?
options: It works, provided that the bilingual paraprofessional speaks the students' home language and attends the ELA block daily.
It works, if the classroom teacher has completed the required ELL-focused CTLE hours for the cycle.
It falls short, because Entering students must receive all of their ENL minutes in Stand-alone classes.
It falls short, because Integrated ENL must be taught by a dually certified teacher or co-taught with an ESOL teacher.
questions.why: Under Part 154, Integrated ENL is delivered either by one teacher certified in both the content area and ESOL, or by a certified content teacher and a certified ESOL teacher co-teaching. A bilingual paraprofessional can be a valuable home-language support, but paraprofessional time does not count toward the required units of study.

traps.note: A bilingual paraprofessional is a valuable support, but paraprofessional time does not count toward ENL units of study, which must be delivered by appropriately certified teachers.
The CTLE rule (at least 15% of PD hours on language acquisition and ELL needs) is professional development for all teachers. It does not qualify a content teacher to deliver Integrated ENL alone.
Right conclusion, wrong reason. K–8 Entering students need 180 Stand-alone minutes AND 180 Integrated ENL/ELA minutes, not all Stand-alone.

questions.key: Integrated ENL = a dually certified teacher, or a certified content teacher co-teaching with a certified ESOL teacher; paraprofessional time doesn't count.

questions.stimulus:
District ELL enrollment, October
Grade | Home language | ELLs districtwide | Most in any one school
K | Spanish | 19 | 19
2 | Bengali | 22 | 9
3 | Arabic | 9 | 6
4 | Arabic | 9 | 5
5 | Arabic | 9 | 6
4 | Urdu, Nepali, Polish, Karen (combined) | 24 | 10
questions.stem: Based on CR Part 154, for which group is the district required to provide a bilingual education program?
options: The kindergarten Spanish speakers, because the whole group attends the same school
The grade 2 Bengali speakers, even though they are spread across several schools
The Arabic speakers in grades 3–5, because together they number more than 20
The grade 4 ELLs who speak Urdu, Nepali, Polish, or Karen, because there are more than 20
questions.why: Part 154 requires a bilingual education program when 20 or more ELLs in the same grade level share the same home language, counted districtwide. The 22 Bengali-speaking second graders meet that threshold even though no single school has 20. The kindergarten group has only 19, the Arabic speakers are spread across three grades, and the grade 4 group does not share one home language. Parents of the Bengali speakers may still choose ENL.

traps.note: Attending one building is a surface detail. Nineteen is below the threshold of 20, so this group does not trigger a required bilingual program.
The count must be within the same grade level. Nine Arabic speakers in each of three grades does not reach 20 in any grade.
The 20 students must share the same home language. Twenty-four ELLs who speak four different languages do not trigger a bilingual program in any one language.

questions.key: Bilingual trigger: 20+ ELLs with the same home language in the same grade, counted districtwide (not per school).

questions.stem: A grade 1 student whose home language is Spanish is identified as an ELL at the Entering level. The district has a two-way Dual Language program in his grade. At the parent orientation, his parents say they would prefer an ENL program. What should the district do?
options: Place him in Dual Language, since Part 154 requires bilingual placement for Entering students when a program exists
Place him in a general education class without ENL, since his parents have declined the bilingual program
Honor the parents' choice and place him in ENL with all the required Stand-alone and Integrated ENL/ELA minutes
Place him in ENL, but in Stand-alone classes only until he reaches the Transitioning level
questions.why: At orientation, parents learn about TBE, Dual Language, and ENL in their preferred language and then choose. If they choose ENL, the student is placed in ENL and receives the units of study for his level. For an Entering student in grades K–8, that is 180 minutes of Stand-alone ENL and 180 minutes of Integrated ENL/ELA each week. Declining a bilingual program is not the same as declining ELL services.

traps.note: Parents choose among the program options. Part 154 does not require bilingual placement at any proficiency level when parents prefer ENL.
Declining a bilingual program is not declining ELL services. The child is still an ELL and must receive ENL at the units required for his level.
A K–8 Entering student needs 180 minutes of Integrated ENL/ELA as well as Stand-alone ENL. Keeping him out of integrated grade-level ELA withholds required access to grade-level instruction.

questions.key: Parents choose TBE, Dual Language, or ENL; if they decline bilingual, the student still gets full ENL services.

questions.stimulus:
Weekly ENL schedules (grades K–8)
Student | Grade | NYSESLAT level | Weekly ENL schedule
Amira | 2 | Entering | 180 min Stand-alone ENL + 180 min Integrated ENL/ELA
Jean-Pierre | 6 | Transitioning | 90 min Integrated ENL/ELA + 90 min Stand-alone ENL
Oksana | 8 | Expanding | 180 min Integrated ENL/science (co-taught)
Tenzin | 3 | Emerging | 180 min Stand-alone ENL + 180 min Integrated ENL/math
questions.stem: An ENL coordinator reviews the weekly schedules above. Which student's schedule falls short of the CR Part 154 minimum?
options: Amira
Jean-Pierre
Oksana
Tenzin
questions.why: A K–8 Emerging student needs 360 minutes a week: 90 minutes of Stand-alone ENL, 180 minutes of Integrated ENL/ELA, and 90 flexible minutes. Tenzin has 360 minutes, but none of his Integrated time is in ELA, so the 180-minute Integrated ENL/ELA requirement is unmet. Amira matches the Entering requirement, Jean-Pierre's flexible 90 may be Stand-alone, and an Expanding student's 180 Integrated minutes may be in ELA or another core content area.

traps.note: Amira's schedule is exactly the Entering requirement: 180 minutes of Stand-alone ENL plus 180 minutes of Integrated ENL/ELA.
A Transitioning student needs 90 minutes of Integrated ENL/ELA plus 90 flexible minutes, and the flexible minutes may be Stand-alone. Jean-Pierre's schedule complies.

traps.pair: Integrated ENL/ELA ↔ Integrated ENL in any content area
traps.note: At the Expanding level, the 180 Integrated minutes may be in ELA or another core content area, so co-taught science is acceptable.

questions.key: Check each component, not just the total: Entering and Emerging students need 180 Integrated ENL minutes specifically in ELA.

questions.stem: A grade 6 student scored at the Transitioning level on the spring NYSESLAT. Which weekly ENL schedule for the next school year meets the CR Part 154 minimum?
options: 90 minutes of Integrated ENL/ELA and 90 minutes of Integrated ENL in social studies
180 minutes of Stand-alone ENL, with no Integrated ENL in any of his classes
90 minutes of Integrated ENL/ELA, with no other ENL services during the week
90 minutes of Stand-alone ENL and 90 minutes of Integrated ENL in mathematics
questions.why: In grades K–8, a Transitioning student receives 180 minutes a week: 90 minutes of Integrated ENL/ELA plus 90 flexible minutes that may be Stand-alone ENL or Integrated ENL in any content area. The first schedule meets both parts. Schedules without Integrated ENL/ELA, or with only 90 total minutes, fall short.

traps.note: The total is right, but 90 of a Transitioning student's minutes must be Integrated ENL/ELA. Only the flexible 90 may be Stand-alone.
Ninety minutes a week is the former-ELL (Commanding) service level. A Transitioning student still needs 180 minutes.
The flexible 90 can be Stand-alone, but the other 90 must be Integrated ENL in ELA specifically. Integrated ENL in math does not substitute for it.

questions.key: K–8 Transitioning = 180 min: 90 Integrated ENL/ELA + 90 flexible (Stand-alone or Integrated).

questions.stem: A grade 4 student scored Commanding on the spring NYSESLAT. Which description of his services for the following school year is consistent with NYS requirements?
options: He exits ELL status and no longer receives ENL support or testing accommodations of any kind.
He continues to receive 180 minutes of ENL until he also scores Level 3 on the Grades 3–8 ELA test.
He receives 90 minutes a week of Integrated ENL or other approved former-ELL services for two years.
He receives former-ELL services for four years, because ESSA keeps former ELs in the subgroup that long.
questions.why: Scoring Commanding on the NYSESLAT exits a student from ELL status, but former ELLs in NYS continue to receive 90 minutes a week of Integrated ENL (or other approved former-ELL services) for two years. They also keep ELL testing accommodations for two years after exit. ESSA's four-year figure concerns accountability reporting, not services.

traps.note: Exiting ELL status doesn't end support. Former ELLs receive continued services and keep testing accommodations for two years after exit.

traps.pair: Commanding exit ↔ Expanding + ELA exit route
traps.note: The ELA-test condition applies only to students who score Expanding. A Commanding score exits a student on its own.
ESSA lets states keep former ELs in the EL subgroup for up to four years for accountability reporting. NYS former-ELL services last two years.

questions.key: Former ELL (Commanding) = 90 min/week of Integrated ENL or approved services, plus accommodations, for 2 years.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the goal of a Transitional Bilingual Education (TBE) program in New York State?
options: Developing bilingualism and biliteracy for ELLs and English-proficient students who learn together in two languages
Using the home language for literacy and content as English increases, so students can move to English-only classes
Providing English language development with a certified ESOL teacher while content is taught in English
Placing ELLs in English-only content classes and using the home language only as a last resort when students are completely lost
questions.why: TBE combines home language arts, content instruction in the home language and English, and ENL. The share of English increases over time, and the goal is to transition students to English-only instruction. Dual Language, by contrast, aims for long-term bilingualism and biliteracy and does not phase out the home language.

traps.note: This describes two-way Dual Language, which aims for biliteracy for all students. TBE serves ELLs and aims to transition them to English-only instruction.
This describes an ENL program. TBE includes ENL, but it also provides home language arts and content instruction in the home language.
This treats the home language as an emergency crutch in an English-only setting. That is the opposite of TBE, which uses the home language systematically to build literacy and content knowledge.

questions.key: TBE: home language + English, with English growing; goal = transition to English-only. Dual Language: goal = bilingualism and biliteracy.

questions.stimulus:
Principal's description at a family open house:
"Our program serves only Spanish-speaking ELLs and former ELLs. Students learn to read and write in both Spanish and English, and science and social studies are taught in both languages. Spanish instruction continues through grade 5 even after students test Commanding, because our goal is for every student to become bilingual and biliterate."
questions.stem: Which program model does the principal's description best match?
options: Transitional Bilingual Education, since the students in the program share the same home language
Two-way Dual Language, since grade-level content is taught in both English and Spanish
Integrated ENL, since former ELLs continue to receive language support in the same classes
One-way Dual Language, since it serves one language group and aims for biliteracy
questions.why: A one-way Dual Language program serves students who are predominantly from one language group and keeps both languages for literacy and content over the long term, because its goal is bilingualism and biliteracy. TBE also serves one language group, but it phases out the home language as English grows. Two-way programs deliberately combine ELLs with English-proficient students.

traps.note: TBE also serves one language group, but it phases out the home language as English grows. Continuing Spanish after students test Commanding, with a biliteracy goal, signals Dual Language.
Both Dual Language models teach in two languages. Two-way programs deliberately include English-proficient students, but this program serves only Spanish-speaking ELLs and former ELLs.
Including former ELLs is a surface detail. Integrated ENL teaches content in English with language support; it does not provide Spanish literacy or aim for biliteracy.

questions.key: One language group + home language kept for biliteracy = one-way Dual Language; home language phased out = TBE.

questions.stem: An ESOL teacher is planning Stand-alone ENL for grade 5 Entering students whose class is starting a science unit on ecosystems. Which plan best reflects the purpose of Stand-alone ENL in New York State?
options: Follow a separate grammar workbook so students master basic structures before they work with science content
Use the period to help the students finish homework assigned in their general education science class
Replace the ecosystems unit with simpler picture books about animals until the students reach Emerging
Teach the English the students need for the unit, such as key vocabulary and patterns for describing food chains
questions.why: In Stand-alone ENL, a certified ESOL teacher provides English language development so that students acquire the English they need to succeed in core content. The strongest Stand-alone lessons are anchored in the content students are studying. Here that means building the vocabulary, sentence structures, and language functions they will use in the ecosystems unit.

traps.note: A grammar sequence detached from content delays access to grade-level learning. Stand-alone ENL should build the English students need for their content classes.
Homework help is useful but reactive. It is not the systematic English language development that Stand-alone ENL exists to provide.
Swapping grade-level science for easier, unrelated texts lowers expectations. NYS expects ELLs to work with grade-level content, with scaffolds.

questions.key: Stand-alone ENL builds the English students need for grade-level content; it is linked to content, not a separate grammar track.

questions.stem: A middle school plans to provide the required ENL minutes for its grade 7 Expanding students through a social studies class co-taught by a certified social studies teacher and a certified ESOL teacher. Which statement about this plan is accurate under CR Part 154?
options: It is acceptable, because an Expanding student's 180 minutes may be Integrated ENL in ELA or another core content area.
It is not acceptable, because Integrated ENL minutes for students at every proficiency level must take place in the ELA class.
It is not acceptable, because Expanding students must also receive at least 90 minutes of Stand-alone ENL.
It is acceptable only if the social studies teacher also holds ESOL certification and teaches the class alone.
questions.why: For K–8 Expanding students, Part 154 requires 180 minutes a week of Integrated ENL, which may be delivered in ELA or another core content area such as social studies. Co-teaching by a certified content teacher and a certified ESOL teacher is one of the two approved ways to deliver Integrated ENL; a single teacher certified in both areas is the other.

traps.note: Entering and Emerging students need Integrated ENL/ELA specifically, and Transitioning students need 90 minutes of it. Expanding students' Integrated ENL may be in any core content area.
There is no Stand-alone minimum at the Expanding level; the required 180 minutes are Integrated ENL.
Co-teaching by a certified content teacher and a certified ESOL teacher is an approved way to deliver Integrated ENL. Dual certification is the other option, not a requirement.

questions.key: K–8 Expanding = 180 min of Integrated ENL in ELA OR another core content area; no Stand-alone minimum.

questions.stem: A grade 2 Entering student whose home language is Chinese is enrolled in a Transitional Bilingual Education (TBE) program. Which statement about her instruction is accurate?
options: She receives no ENL, because part of her content instruction is delivered in her home language.
She receives home language arts, content instruction in both languages, and ENL for her level.
She is taught in Chinese, with English instruction added once she reaches the Expanding level.
She receives content instruction in English, and Chinese is used mainly for parent meetings.
questions.why: NYS bilingual programs (TBE and Dual Language) combine three parts: home language arts, content instruction in both the home language and English, and ENL. Students in a bilingual program still receive ENL units of study for their proficiency level, so the program develops both languages from the start.

traps.note: Students in bilingual programs still receive ENL for their proficiency level. Home-language content instruction does not replace English language development.
TBE develops both languages from the start. It is not home-language-only instruction until the student reaches a set English level.
English-only content instruction describes an ENL program, not TBE, which teaches content in the home language as well as English.

questions.key: Bilingual programs (TBE, Dual Language) = home language arts + content in both languages + ENL.

questions.stem: A district enrolls six Pashto-speaking ELLs in grade 5 and no other Pashto speakers in that grade. A parent asks the district to create a Pashto bilingual class. Which response is accurate under CR Part 154?
options: A bilingual program is required only when 20 or more same-grade ELLs share a home language districtwide, so the student receives ENL.
The district must open a Pashto bilingual class, because a parent has formally requested one in writing.
The student should attend general education classes without ENL until enough Pashto speakers enroll to form a bilingual program.
The student should receive ENL, and teachers should avoid Pashto in class so she is not confused by two languages.
questions.why: A bilingual program is mandated when 20 or more ELLs in the same grade share a home language districtwide. Six students do not reach that threshold, so the student receives ENL at the units required for her level. ENL teachers can still use Pashto as an asset through bilingual glossaries, home-language texts, and translanguaging.

traps.note: A parent request alone doesn't trigger a required bilingual program. The trigger is 20 or more ELLs with the same home language in the same grade, districtwide.
Every identified ELL must be served now. Withholding ENL while waiting for a bilingual program denies the student required instruction.
Two languages don't confuse learners; the home language is a resource. ENL teachers can use Pashto texts, glossaries, and translanguaging even without a bilingual program.

questions.key: Fewer than 20 same-language, same-grade ELLs districtwide: provide ENL, and still use the home language as an asset.

questions.stimulus:
Observation notes, grade 1 Stand-alone ENL (Entering students):
The teacher says, "Stand up," stands up herself, and the students copy her. "Touch your nose. Touch your knees. Walk to the door." After several rounds she gives the commands without modeling them, then in new combinations: "Walk to the window and touch your nose." The students respond only with actions; no one is asked to speak.
questions.stem: The teacher's lesson best reflects which method?
options: The Silent Way
Total Physical Response
The Audiolingual Method
The Direct Method
questions.why: Total Physical Response (James Asher) links language to movement. The teacher gives commands and models them, and students show comprehension through physical action before they are asked to speak. Recombining commands in new ways keeps students listening for meaning. Because it builds listening comprehension with low anxiety, it suits Entering students and young learners.

traps.note: In the Silent Way the teacher says as little as possible and students do the talking, prompted by rods and charts. Here the teacher talks constantly and students respond only with actions.
Audiolingual lessons require students to repeat and drill spoken patterns. These students never speak; they show comprehension through movement.
The Direct Method also stays in English and uses demonstration, but students answer questions in full sentences. Commands answered with physical actions are TPR's signature.

questions.key: Commands + physical responses + no forced speech = Total Physical Response (Asher).

questions.stimulus:
Classroom transcript, grade 9 Stand-alone ENL:
T: Listen and repeat. "I am going to the store."
Ss: I am going to the store.
T: Good! "She."
Ss: She is going to the store.
T: Excellent! "They."
Ss: They is going—
T: No. They ARE going. Again.
Ss: They are going to the store.
T: Very good! "The library."
Ss: They are going to the library.
questions.stem: This exchange most clearly reflects which method?
options: Communicative Language Teaching
The Direct Method
The Audiolingual Method
Grammar-Translation
questions.why: The Audiolingual Method uses substitution drills, choral repetition, immediate correction, and praise to build accurate habits. It rests on Skinner's behaviorism (stimulus, response, reinforcement) and on structural linguistics, so language is practiced as habit formation. No real message is communicated; students manipulate a pattern.

traps.note: CLT centers on meaningful communication and negotiation of meaning. These students exchange no real information; they manipulate a sentence pattern.
The Direct Method is also oral and English-only, but it builds language through question-and-answer exchanges about objects and pictures, not mechanical substitution drills reinforced with praise.
Grammar-Translation relies on written translation and explicit rule explanation, often in the home language. This lesson is entirely oral drilling.

questions.key: Substitution drills + repetition + immediate reinforcement = Audiolingual Method, rooted in behaviorism.

questions.stem: A high school ESOL teacher says that her instruction follows Communicative Language Teaching (CLT). Which activity is most consistent with that approach?
options: Students repeat a model dialogue about ordering food until they can say it without any errors.
Students translate a news article into their home language and list its new grammar structures.
Students copy the rules for the present perfect and complete a fill-in-the-blank worksheet.
Students plan a weekend outing in pairs, using real event listings, and explain their choice.
questions.why: CLT grows out of Hymes's concept of communicative competence: the goal is using language appropriately for real purposes. Activities use authentic materials and require students to exchange information, negotiate, and make decisions. Fluency is valued, and grammar is taught in service of communication. Planning an outing from real listings requires all of this.

traps.note: Memorizing and repeating a dialogue until it is error-free is Audiolingual habit formation; no real information is exchanged.
Translating and listing structures is Grammar-Translation. It builds knowledge about English, not the ability to communicate in it.
Copying rules and filling in blanks practices form in isolation, with no communicative purpose or audience.

questions.key: CLT = real communicative purpose, information exchange, negotiation, and fluency, not drills, translation, or rule copying.

questions.stem: A grade 3 ENL teacher fills her lessons with comprehensible input: pictures, gestures, and slow, clear stories. She does not require newer students to speak until they are ready. She asks them yes/no and either/or questions ("Is this an apple or a banana?"), and she responds to the meaning of their one-word answers without correcting their form. Which approach does her practice best reflect?
options: The Natural Approach
Total Physical Response
The Direct Method
Suggestopedia
questions.why: The Natural Approach (Krashen & Terrell) puts Krashen's hypotheses into practice. It floods students with comprehensible input, allows a silent (preproduction) period, and keeps the affective filter low by not correcting errors in early stages. Questions are matched to the stage, such as yes/no and either/or questions for students moving into early production. TPR activities may be used within it, but these features define the Natural Approach.

traps.note: TPR also delays speech, but its core is commands answered with physical actions. Stories, stage-matched questions, and tolerance of errors define the Natural Approach, which may borrow TPR activities.
The Direct Method stays in English but expects full-sentence answers and accurate pronunciation from the start. It does not build in a silent period.
Suggestopedia lowers anxiety with music, comfortable surroundings, and positive suggestion while presenting long dialogues. None of those features appears here.

questions.key: Comprehensible input + no forced speech + stage-matched questions + tolerance of errors = Natural Approach (Krashen & Terrell).

questions.stimulus:
Observation notes, grade 10 Stand-alone ENL:
The teacher says almost nothing. She points to colored wooden rods of different lengths and to a wall chart of color-coded sounds. When a student says, "Take a red rod," she nods. When another student mispronounces "rod," she silently points to the vowel on the chart and waits; a classmate helps him correct it.
questions.stem: Which method is the teacher using?
options: Total Physical Response
Suggestopedia
Community Language Learning
The Silent Way
questions.why: In Gattegno's Silent Way, the teacher stays mostly silent so that students do most of the talking. She uses Cuisenaire rods and color-coded sound charts as prompts. Learning is treated as discovery and problem solving: students are expected to self-correct and help one another instead of imitating a teacher model.

traps.note: TPR teachers talk constantly, giving commands that students act out. Here the teacher is nearly silent and the students produce the language.
Suggestopedia uses music, relaxation, and long dialogues read by the teacher. It is input-rich and teacher-voiced, the opposite of a silent teacher.
In CLL the teacher actively supplies English versions of what learners want to say. The Silent Way teacher withholds models so that learners discover and self-correct.

questions.key: Mostly silent teacher + Cuisenaire rods + color-coded charts + self-correction = Silent Way (Gattegno).

questions.stem: In a teacher's ESOL class, students spend most of their time translating literary passages between English and their home languages and memorizing grammar rules and bilingual vocabulary lists. What is the most significant limitation of this approach for ELLs in U.S. schools?
options: It gives students little practice using English orally to communicate and to learn in content classes.
It relies too heavily on the home language, which delays the students' acquisition of English.
It focuses on literary texts instead of the grammar that students need to pass their tests.
It teaches grammar inductively, so students do not learn the rules of English explicitly.
questions.why: This is Grammar-Translation: grammar is taught deductively through explicit rules and applied in written translation, with emphasis on reading and writing accuracy. It builds knowledge about the language but gives almost no practice in listening, speaking, or using English to communicate, which is exactly what ELLs need for social and academic success. Using the home language is not itself the problem.

traps.note: Using the home language is not the problem; it can be a powerful resource. The weakness is that translation work leaves little time for communicative English.
Grammar-Translation is grammar-heavy and teaches rules explicitly. Latching onto 'literary passages' misses its real limitation.
Grammar-Translation is deductive: the rule comes first, then practice. Inductive grammar (discovering rules from examples) belongs to methods such as the Direct Method.

questions.key: Grammar-Translation = deductive rules + translation + reading and writing; its major gap is oral, communicative use.

questions.stimulus:
Observation notes, grade 8 Stand-alone ENL:
The teacher uses only English and never translates. She holds up a pencil and asks, "What is this?" A student answers, "It is a pencil." "Is it a book?" "No, it is not a book. It is a pencil." She places the pencil on, under, and next to a desk, asking questions so that students work out how the prepositions are used; she never states a rule. She insists on full-sentence answers and correct pronunciation. Later, students write short sentences about the objects.
questions.stem: Which method do these practices most closely reflect?
options: The Audiolingual Method
The Direct Method
The Natural Approach
Total Physical Response
questions.why: The Direct Method teaches only in the target language through demonstration, realia, and question-and-answer exchanges. Grammar is taught inductively, and accurate pronunciation and full-sentence answers are emphasized; writing follows oral work. The Audiolingual Method also avoids translation, but it relies on memorized dialogues and mechanical pattern drills reinforced by praise, not Q&A about real objects.

traps.note: ALM also avoids translation, but it relies on dialogue memorization and pattern drills reinforced by praise. Q&A about real objects, inductive grammar, and follow-up writing point to the Direct Method.
The Natural Approach accepts one-word answers and avoids correcting form in early stages. Insisting on full sentences and correct pronunciation is not Natural Approach practice.
Moving a pencil around a desk is a surface detail. In TPR, students carry out commands physically; here the teacher manipulates the objects and students answer questions.

questions.key: English-only Q&A with objects and pictures + inductive grammar + full-sentence accuracy = Direct Method.

questions.stem: A department chair proposes that ELLs complete a sequence of English grammar courses before they take grade-level science and social studies. Which response best reflects the principles of Content-Based Instruction (CBI)?
options: ELLs can develop academic English and content knowledge at the same time, because content gives language a real purpose.
ELLs should take the grammar courses first, with lists of science and history vocabulary added to each grammar lesson.
ELLs should begin content courses once they reach Transitioning, when they can follow lectures in English.
ELLs should take content courses right away, using simplified materials from earlier grade levels.
questions.why: Content-Based Instruction integrates language and content: students acquire English while learning grade-level subject matter, because content provides meaningful, cognitively engaging input and real reasons to use language. Sheltered models such as SIOP, and CALLA, build on this principle. Postponing content until English is 'ready' costs ELLs years of academic learning.

traps.note: Adding word lists to a grammar sequence still teaches language apart from content. CBI teaches language through meaningful content.
Waiting for a proficiency level withholds years of grade-level content. CBI's premise is that language develops through content, not before it.
CBI keeps grade-level concepts and scaffolds access to them. Lower-grade materials water down the content.

questions.key: CBI: learn English through grade-level content; language and content develop together, so don't wait for English first.

questions.stimulus:
Observation notes, grade 11 Stand-alone ENL:
Students sit in a circle around an audio recorder. A student quietly says in Ukrainian what she wants to tell the group. The teacher, standing behind her, gives the English version, and the student repeats it into the recorder. After the conversation, the class listens to the recording, the teacher writes the English sentences on the board for discussion, and students talk about how they felt during the activity.
questions.stem: Which method is the teacher using?
options: Suggestopedia
The Grammar-Translation Method
Community Language Learning
The Silent Way
questions.why: In Curran's Community Language Learning, the teacher acts as a counselor or 'knower' who translates what learners want to say. Learners repeat the English version, the conversation is recorded and transcribed for analysis, and students reflect on their feelings. Drawing on humanistic counseling, it builds trust, reduces anxiety, and lets learners control the content.

traps.note: Both are humanistic methods that aim to reduce anxiety, but Suggestopedia uses music, relaxation, and teacher-presented dialogues. Learner-generated talk translated by a teacher-counselor and then recorded is CLL.
Translation appears here, but it is oral, on demand, and serves the learners' own messages. Grammar-Translation translates written texts and teaches rules.
The Silent Way teacher withholds language. This teacher supplies the English version of everything the learner wants to say.

questions.key: Learner says it in the home language, teacher-counselor gives the English, talk is recorded and transcribed, then reflection = CLL (Curran).

questions.stem: A grade 9 ENL teacher builds a unit around one outcome: small groups use real bus and subway schedules and a fixed budget to produce a workable itinerary for a class trip. First, students listen to a model planning conversation. After the groups present their itineraries, the class studies language they needed, such as modals for making suggestions. Which approach does this unit most specifically reflect?
options: Communicative Language Teaching
Task-Based Language Teaching
Content-Based Instruction
The Language Experience Approach
questions.why: Task-Based Language Teaching organizes instruction around meaningful tasks with a non-linguistic outcome, here a workable itinerary. A typical cycle is pre-task (a model or preparation), the task itself in groups, a report, and then a language focus on forms students needed. TBLT is a strong version of CLT, but the task-and-outcome structure is what identifies it specifically.

traps.note: TBLT is a form of CLT, so CLT isn't wrong, but it is the broad umbrella. A unit built on a task with a concrete outcome, followed by a language focus, is specifically TBLT.
CBI teaches language through academic subject matter such as science or history. Planning a trip itinerary is a real-world task, not a content course.
In the LEA, students' dictated account of a shared experience becomes their reading material. Nothing here turns students' words into a text to read.

questions.key: A unit built around a real-world task with an outcome, followed by a language focus = Task-Based Language Teaching.

questions.stimulus:
Lesson-plan excerpt, grade 6 Integrated ENL science (SIOP):
- Ask students to describe how their families kept food cold or fresh without a refrigerator; connect their answers to today's topic, heat transfer.
- Display last week's anchor chart on conduction and have partners explain how it connects to today's lesson.
- Introduce and post the key terms insulator, conductor, and transfer, each with a picture.
questions.stem: These planned activities most directly address which SIOP component?
options: Lesson Preparation
Comprehensible Input
Building Background
Review & Assessment
questions.why: SIOP's Building Background component has three features: linking concepts to students' background experiences, explicitly linking past learning to new concepts, and emphasizing key vocabulary. All three appear here: the family food-storage connection, last week's anchor chart, and the posted key terms. Comprehensible Input is about how the teacher speaks, explains tasks, and uses techniques such as modeling during instruction.

traps.note: Lesson Preparation covers writing content and language objectives, choosing appropriate concepts, and adapting materials. It is the planning itself, not linking to students' experiences and prior learning.

Visuals appear here, but Comprehensible Input concerns how the teacher speaks, explains tasks, and uses techniques during instruction. Connecting to experiences, past learning, and key vocabulary is Building Background.

Review & Assessment comes at the end of a lesson: reviewing today's vocabulary and concepts, giving feedback, and checking learning. Using last week's chart to launch new learning is Building Background.

questions.key: SIOP Building Background = connect to students' experiences + link past learning to new + emphasize key vocabulary.

questions.stimulus:
Unit overview, grade 8 Integrated ENL math:
Preparation: Students discuss how they usually attack word problems.
Presentation: The teacher names and models the strategy "selective attention," thinking aloud as she underlines the question and the key quantities.
Practice: Partners apply the strategy to grade-level problems.
Self-evaluation: Students rate whether the strategy helped them and explain why.
Expansion: Students identify other classes where the strategy could help them.
questions.stem: This unit design most specifically reflects which approach?
options: The SIOP Model
Task-Based Language Teaching
The Language Experience Approach
CALLA
questions.why: Chamot and O'Malley's Cognitive Academic Language Learning Approach (CALLA) integrates grade-level content, academic language, and explicit instruction in learning strategies (metacognitive, cognitive, and social/affective). Its five-phase sequence of preparation, presentation, practice, self-evaluation, and expansion appears here exactly. SIOP includes a Strategies component, but SIOP is a broader eight-component planning and observation model.

traps.note: SIOP does include a Strategies component, but it is an eight-component lesson-planning and observation model. An explicit five-phase strategy-instruction cycle is CALLA's signature.
TBLT is organized around a task with a real-world outcome. This unit is organized around explicitly teaching, practicing, and evaluating a learning strategy.
The LEA turns students' dictated experiences into reading text. It doesn't involve explicit strategy instruction in a content area.

questions.key: Content + academic language + explicit strategy instruction in five phases (prepare, present, practice, self-evaluate, expand) = CALLA.

questions.stem: A grade 9 ENL teacher works with SIFE who are beginning to read in English. After a class visit to a community garden, she wants reading material that the students can understand and that builds on their own words and experiences. Which approach best fits her goal?
options: Total Physical Response: students act out the steps of planting as the teacher gives commands
The Audiolingual Method: students repeat garden vocabulary chorally until pronunciation is accurate
The Language Experience Approach: students tell about the visit as the teacher writes their words to read
Grammar-Translation: students translate a published article about gardens into their home languages
questions.why: In the Language Experience Approach, a shared experience becomes text. Students describe it, the teacher writes their words (often on a chart), and the class reads, rereads, and works with that text. Because it uses the students' own language and experiences, the text is highly comprehensible and motivating, which makes it an effective bridge to literacy for SIFE and beginning readers of any age.

traps.note: TPR can build oral comprehension of garden vocabulary, but it produces no reading material, which is the teacher's stated goal.
Choral vocabulary drills are decontextualized and don't create a comprehensible text built from the students' experience.
Translating a published article demands strong literacy in two languages, which beginning readers with interrupted schooling may not yet have, and it doesn't use their own words.

questions.key: Shared experience → students dictate → teacher writes → the text becomes reading material = Language Experience Approach.

questions.stem: A grade 5 Integrated ENL/ELA class includes students whose home languages are Spanish, Bengali, and Arabic; the two co-teachers speak English and Spanish. They want to apply translanguaging pedagogy during a unit on a grade-level novel. Which plan best reflects this approach?
options: Allow students to use their home languages only when they are completely lost, and then redirect them back to English right away.
Have students discuss chapters in same-language pairs, take notes in any language, and then draft responses in English.
Give students the novel in their home languages so they can read those editions in place of the English text.
Use Spanish with the Spanish speakers only, since the teachers cannot support Bengali or Arabic in class.
questions.why: Translanguaging pedagogy (Ofelia García; CUNY-NYSIEB) treats students' languages as one linguistic repertoire and deliberately plans for them to use all of it to learn: discussing, note-taking, and drafting. Students can then engage grade-level texts more deeply and produce in English. Teachers do not need to speak every home language; they design structures such as same-language partners and multilingual resources.

traps.note: Treating the home language as an emergency crutch to be phased out is the opposite of translanguaging, which plans home-language use as a resource for learning.
Home-language editions can be a useful support, but replacing the English text removes the grade-level English reading students need. Translanguaging uses the languages together.

Translanguaging doesn't require teachers to speak every language. Teachers design structures, such as same-language partners and multilingual resources, that let all students use their full repertoires.

questions.key: Translanguaging = planned use of students' full linguistic repertoire for learning; teachers needn't speak every language.

questions.stimulus:
Lesson plan, grade 4 Integrated ENL science (Emerging to Expanding students)
Content objective: Students will describe the four stages of a butterfly's life cycle.
Activities: Students watch a time-lapse video, sort picture cards into order, and explain the cycle to a partner.
questions.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate language objective for this lesson?
options: Students will learn the stages of a butterfly's life cycle by watching a time-lapse video.
Students will orally sequence the life cycle stages using first, next, then, and finally.
Students will complete a picture-sorting activity about the life cycle with a partner.
Students will spell egg, larva, pupa, and adult correctly on a vocabulary quiz.
questions.why: A language objective names the language function students will use (here, sequencing), the domain (speaking), and the forms that support it (sequence words). That makes it observable and directly tied to the content objective. Strong language objectives state how students will use language to learn and show the content; activities and restated content goals do not.

traps.note: This restates the content goal and adds an activity. It says nothing about the language students will use to show their learning.
Sorting cards is an activity, not an objective. It doesn't name the language function or forms students will learn.
Spelling words on a quiz is language-related, but it is isolated from the lesson's real language demand (explaining a sequence) and from meaningful use.

questions.key: Language objective = function + domain + supporting forms (e.g., orally sequence using first/next/then), tied to the content objective.

questions.stem: A teacher writes this language objective: "Students will compare two habitats in writing, using comparative adjectives (-er than, more … than) and the conjunction whereas." Which element of the objective is the language function?
options: compare
comparative adjectives and whereas
two habitats
in writing
questions.why: A language function is the purpose for which language is used: describe, compare, explain, sequence, argue. Language forms are the grammatical structures and vocabulary that carry out the function, here comparative adjectives and whereas. Writing is the domain, and habitats are the content.

traps.note: Comparative adjectives and whereas are forms: the structures students use to carry out the function.
Habitats are the content topic, not what students do with language.
Writing is the domain (along with listening, speaking, and reading), not the function.

questions.key: Function = purpose (compare, explain); forms = structures and vocabulary that do it; domain = listening, speaking, reading, or writing.

questions.stimulus:
Writing task, grade 8 Integrated ENL social studies:
"Were the colonists justified in protesting the Stamp Act? Write a paragraph that states your claim and supports it with evidence from Documents A and B."
questions.stem: As she plans, the ESOL co-teacher analyzes the language demands of this task. Which analysis is most complete?
options: Students will read Documents A and B, so the main demand is the readability level of the two sources.
Students need the words justified, protest, and Stamp Act, so the main demand is at the word level.
Students must argue: state a claim, cite evidence from each document, and connect it to the claim.
Students will need to spell and punctuate correctly, so the main demand is formal paragraph conventions.
questions.why: Analyzing language demands means looking beyond vocabulary to the function and the discourse- and sentence-level structures a task requires. This task calls for argument: a claim, cited evidence ('According to Document A…'), and reasoning that links them with connectors such as because and therefore. Vocabulary and readability matter, but they are only parts of the demand; the teacher should plan supports for the argument structure itself.

traps.note: Readability matters for the reading part, but it ignores what students must produce: a written argument with claim, evidence, and reasoning.
Key vocabulary is one layer of the demand, but word-level analysis misses the discourse and sentence structures that argument requires.
Conventions are surface features. Focusing on spelling and punctuation misses the function (argue) and the structures the task demands.

questions.key: Analyze language demands at the word, sentence, and discourse levels, starting with the function (e.g., argue) the task requires.

questions.stem: In a grade 6 Integrated ENL/ELA class, all students will write a paragraph explaining how a character changes in a grade-level short story. Which plan best matches supports to an Emerging student and an Expanding student?
options: Both: the same paragraph frame and the same word bank, so that the task is equally fair for each of them
Emerging: copy a model paragraph from the board; Expanding: write with no supports
Emerging: partly completed organizer, word bank, and frames; Expanding: complex-sentence starters
Emerging: an easier story with a different character; Expanding: the grade-level story
questions.why: The NYS New Language Arts Progressions describe the same grade-level task at each level, with support that decreases as proficiency rises. An Emerging student can explain character change with substantial support: an organizer, a word bank, and sentence frames. An Expanding student needs lighter, targeted support to produce complex, cohesive sentences. Both work with the same grade-level text and standard.

traps.note: Identical supports ignore the difference in proficiency: the Expanding student is under-challenged, and the Emerging student may need more.
Copying a model produces no original thinking or language, and Expanding students still benefit from targeted support for complex language.
An easier, different text removes the Emerging student's access to the grade-level text and standard. Scaffold the same text instead.

questions.key: Same grade-level task; heavier supports (frames, word banks, organizers) for Emerging and lighter, targeted supports for Expanding.

questions.stem: A grade 7 Entering student whose home language is Dari has just joined a social studies class that is studying ancient Mesopotamia. Which plan for his first weeks best supports his access to the grade-level content?
options: Give him coloring pages of animals to complete while the class works, until he learns basic English.
Have him complete the same essay assignment as his classmates, so that he is not singled out.
Schedule extra Stand-alone ENL for him during social studies until he reaches the Transitioning level.
Provide a labeled map, visuals, a bilingual glossary, home-language resources, and a partner for sorts.
questions.why: Entering students can engage with grade-level concepts when the language load is supported. Visuals, labeled maps, home-language resources, bilingual glossaries, and structured partner work let him build content knowledge and English at the same time. Unrelated busywork or removal from the class delays learning, and an unsupported essay ignores his proficiency level.

traps.note: Unrelated busywork withholds grade-level content and signals low expectations.
The same unsupported essay ignores his Entering level. He needs scaffolds to show what he understands.
Pulling him out of social studies removes him from grade-level content. Entering students learn content and English together, with support.

questions.key: Entering students: keep the grade-level content and add heavy visual, home-language, and partner supports.

questions.stimulus:
Lesson plan, grade 3 Integrated ENL/ELA (Emerging and Transitioning students)
1. Teacher thinks aloud while writing a summary of a short informational text.
2. Students independently write a summary of a new text.
3. Teacher collects and grades the summaries.
questions.stem: Based on the gradual release of responsibility model, which revision would most strengthen this plan?
options: Add a second teacher think-aloud so students see two complete models before writing on their own.
Add a summary written jointly with the class, then partner practice, before students write alone.
Replace the summary with a vocabulary-matching worksheet, which is more manageable for Emerging students.
Add a spelling test on the text's key words before students begin to write their summaries.
questions.why: Gradual release moves from 'I do' (teacher modeling) to 'we do' (guided, shared practice) to 'you do together' (collaborative practice) to 'you do alone' (independent work). This plan jumps from modeling straight to independent writing, skipping the guided and collaborative stages where ELLs rehearse the language and get feedback. More modeling alone still leaves that gap.

traps.note: Another model can help, but the plan would still jump from 'I do' to 'you do alone' with no guided or collaborative practice.
Swapping summarizing for matching lowers the cognitive demand. Scaffold the summary instead.
A spelling test is decontextualized and does nothing to build the skill of summarizing.

questions.key: Gradual release: I do → we do → you do together → you do alone. Don't jump from modeling to independence.

questions.stem: An ESOL teacher and a grade 5 teacher are co-planning a unit using backward design (Understanding by Design). What should they do first?
options: Identify the desired results: the standards-based content and language goals for the unit
Choose engaging activities and materials that will keep the ELLs motivated across the unit
Give a pretest to group the students by proficiency level before choosing any unit goals
Select the textbook chapters to be covered and pace them across the unit calendar
questions.why: Backward design (Wiggins & McTighe) has three stages: (1) identify desired results, (2) determine acceptable evidence of learning, and (3) plan learning experiences and instruction. For ELLs, the desired results include both the content goals and the language students need to reach them, so language objectives grow out of stage 1.

traps.note: Engagement matters, but in backward design activities are chosen last, after the goals and the assessment evidence are set.
Pre-assessment data helps with differentiation, but backward design begins with the goals, not with grouping.
Planning by textbook coverage is the 'forward' habit that backward design was created to replace.

questions.key: Backward design: (1) desired results → (2) assessment evidence → (3) learning activities.

questions.stem: A grade 7 science teacher's language objective is "Students will orally explain the causes of the seasons to a partner using because and as a result." Which assessment is best aligned with this objective?
options: A multiple-choice quiz on the causes of the seasons, given to the whole class at the end of the lesson
A matching activity that pairs season vocabulary words with their definitions
A written paragraph about the seasons, graded for spelling and punctuation
A partner explanation, monitored with a checklist for accuracy and the target phrases
questions.why: In backward design, the assessment evidence must match the objective. This objective names a domain (speaking), a function (explaining causes), and forms (because, as a result), so the evidence should be an oral explanation checked against those criteria. A quiz, a matching task, or a paragraph graded for conventions measures something else.

traps.note: A multiple-choice quiz checks recognition of content, not the oral explanation or the target forms named in the objective.
Matching words to definitions tests isolated vocabulary, not explaining causes orally with because and as a result.
This measures writing conventions, a different domain and different criteria from the speaking objective.

questions.key: Assess what the objective names: the same domain, the same function, and the same target forms.

questions.stem: A grade 10 ESOL teacher co-teaches a global history class. The content teacher suggests replacing the grade-level reading on the causes of World War I with a short, simplified summary for the Emerging students. Which response best reflects effective scaffolding for ELLs?
options: Keep the grade-level text, but chunk it, pre-teach key concepts, add glosses and visuals, and pose guiding questions.
Agree to the plan, because simplified texts let Emerging students learn the content without becoming frustrated by it.
Keep the grade-level text, and have the Emerging students reread it silently until they can understand it.
Give the Emerging students a summary in their home languages, so they do not need to read the English text.
questions.why: Effective scaffolding amplifies rather than simplifies (Walqui): students keep access to complex, grade-level text while the teacher adds temporary supports such as chunking, pre-teaching key concepts, glosses, visuals, and guiding questions. Simplified summaries often strip out the connectors and academic language students need to learn, which lowers rigor.

traps.note: Simplified summaries often strip out the connectors and academic language students need to learn, and they lower expectations.
Unsupported rereading assumes an independence Emerging students don't yet have. They need substantial, planned scaffolds.
Home-language resources are a valuable bridge, but replacing the English text removes the grade-level English reading students need to develop.

questions.key: Scaffold, don't simplify: keep the grade-level text and add temporary supports (chunking, glosses, visuals, guiding questions).

questions.stem: Since September, a grade 4 teacher has given her Expanding students the same fill-in frame ("The character felt ___ because ___.") for every written response. In January, their responses are accurate but nearly identical, and they rarely go beyond the frame. What is the best next step?
options: Keep using the same frame, since the students are now producing accurate sentences with it.
Remove all supports at once, so that the students are pushed to write fully on their own.
Switch to a longer frame that has more blanks, so that the students produce more writing.
Fade the frame: offer open starters and a menu of connectors, then move toward independence.
questions.why: Scaffolds are temporary by design. As proficiency grows, the teacher gradually releases responsibility, moving from fill-in frames to open starters and connector banks and then to independent writing. A frame that never changes can cap students' production, while removing all support at once leaves them without a bridge.

traps.note: Accuracy within a frame is good, but a scaffold that never changes caps growth. Expanding students need to move toward varied, independent writing.
Abrupt removal skips the bridge. Expanding students still benefit from light, targeted support while it fades.
More blanks produce longer responses, but students are still filling in someone else's sentence. The issue is independence, not length.

questions.key: Scaffolds are temporary: fade them gradually as proficiency grows (frame → starters → connector bank → independent).

questions.stem: A grade 2 class is learning to identify and describe two-dimensional shapes. Which language objective is most appropriate for the Entering students in the class?
options: Students will write a paragraph comparing triangles and squares using complex sentences.
Students will name shapes and tell how many sides each has, using "It has __ sides" and pictures.
Students will listen quietly as classmates describe shapes, so they can absorb the vocabulary.
Students will copy the names of ten two-dimensional shapes from the board into notebooks.
questions.why: Language objectives should target the same grade-level content while matching expectations to proficiency. Entering students can name and describe using words, short phrases, and simple frames with visual support. A paragraph of complex comparisons is beyond the Entering level, while silent listening or copying offers no meaningful output.

traps.note: A paragraph of complex comparative sentences fits Expanding or Commanding students, not Entering students.
Listening matters, but an objective with no output gives Entering students no chance to use the new language.
Copying words is rote and decontextualized; students never use language to describe the shapes.

questions.key: Entering language objectives: same content, words and phrases with frames and visuals; meaningful output, not copying or silence.

questions.stimulus:
Text excerpt, grade 8 science:
"Because wolves were removed from the park, the elk population, which had previously been kept in check, grew rapidly, resulting in the overgrazing of willow trees along the rivers."
questions.stem: When planning, the ESOL teacher wants to address the sentence-level language demands of this excerpt. Which demand should she prioritize?
options: The technical word overgrazing, which many students may not know or be able to define
A cause-and-effect chain packed into an embedded clause and a participial phrase
The past tense verbs were and grew, which signal a narrative
The phrase kept in check, which students may read literally
questions.why: Sentence-level demands come from how ideas are packaged grammatically. This sentence embeds a relative clause (which had previously been kept in check) and ends with a participial phrase (resulting in…) that carries a chain of causes and effects. Teachers can scaffold by unpacking it into shorter sentences and then rebuilding it, so students learn to read and eventually write such sentences.

traps.note: Overgrazing is a real word-level demand, but the question asks about the sentence level: how ideas are packaged grammatically.
The simple past verbs aren't the challenge, and the excerpt is a cause-and-effect explanation, not a narrative.
Kept in check is a phrase-level (idiomatic) demand worth teaching, but the larger sentence-level challenge is the clause structure.

questions.key: Sentence-level demands = complex structures (embedded clauses, participial phrases). Unpack them, then repack them.

questions.stem: What is the primary reason for writing a language objective in addition to a content objective for a lesson that includes ELLs?
options: To make explicit the language students need to learn the content, so that it is taught and assessed
To give ELLs a separate and easier objective in place of the grade-level content objective
To satisfy a lesson-plan format requirement for formal observations by administrators
To identify the grammar rules that students will practice in isolation after the content part of the lesson
questions.why: Language objectives make the language of the lesson visible: the functions, forms, and vocabulary students need in order to understand and demonstrate the content. Naming them ensures that this language is deliberately taught, practiced, and assessed alongside the content rather than assumed. Every student benefits, not only ELLs.

traps.note: Language objectives accompany the grade-level content objective; they don't replace it with an easier one.
Format compliance is a surface reason. The real purpose is to make language teaching deliberate.
Language objectives are tied to the lesson's content and tasks, not to grammar practice in isolation.

questions.key: Language objectives make lesson-specific language explicit so that it is taught and assessed alongside (not instead of) content.

questions.stem: During the collaborative ("you do it together") stage of a grade 5 lesson on opinion paragraphs, an ESOL teacher notices that three Emerging students cannot yet state a reason using because, while the rest of the class is working well. What is the most effective response?
options: Move the whole class back to teacher modeling so that everyone hears the explanation again.
Let the three students skip the reason and write only their opinion, to keep the task manageable.
Pull the three into a brief guided group to build reasons with because, then return them to partners.
Let the three keep working with partners, since struggling at this stage builds independence.
questions.why: Gradual release is recursive, not a one-way march. When formative evidence shows that some students aren't ready, the teacher temporarily returns those students to guided instruction while the others continue. A targeted small group keeps the Emerging students working toward the full grade-level task (opinion plus reason) within their zone of proximal development.

traps.note: Reteaching everyone wastes time for students who are ready. The evidence points to a targeted group.
Dropping the reason removes the core of opinion writing. Scaffold the reason instead.
Productive struggle helps only within the zone of proximal development. These students lack the language they need even with peers, so they need more guided support.

questions.key: Gradual release is recursive: re-teach students who aren't ready in a guided small group while the others continue.

questions.stimulus:
Grade 4 Integrated ENL/ELA, morning share:
Student (Emerging; home language Haitian Creole): Yesterday I go to the library with my brother.
Teacher: Oh, you went to the library with your brother yesterday? What did you find there?
Student: I find—I found a book about sharks!
questions.stem: The teacher's response is an example of which type of corrective feedback?
options: Explicit correction
Elicitation
Metalinguistic feedback
Recast
questions.why: A recast reformulates all or part of a student's utterance correctly (go → went) without saying that an error occurred, so the focus stays on meaning. Lyster and Ranta found that recasts are the most frequent type of teacher feedback. They are unobtrusive, though students don't always notice them. Here the student does notice and self-corrects, which is called uptake.

traps.note: Explicit correction clearly signals the error and gives the correct form ('Not go: went'). This teacher gives no signal; she simply reformulates.
Elicitation pushes the student to produce the form himself, by pausing or asking. This teacher supplies the correct form.
Metalinguistic feedback comments on the grammar ('Yesterday means past tense'). No grammatical information is given here.

questions.key: Recast = the teacher reformulates the error correctly, with no explicit signal that an error occurred.

questions.stimulus:
Grade 6 Stand-alone ENL:
Student (Transitioning; home language Mandarin): My sister have two cats.
Teacher: My sister …? (pauses and waits)
Student: My sister has two cats.
questions.stem: Which type of corrective feedback did the teacher use?
options: Repetition
Elicitation
Recast
Clarification request
questions.why: Elicitation prompts students to produce the correct form themselves. The teacher may pause so the student completes the utterance ('My sister …?'), ask 'How do we say that?', or ask the student to reformulate. Repetition, by contrast, repeats the student's error, usually with rising intonation ('My sister have?'). Elicitation tends to lead to student-generated repair.

traps.note: Repetition repeats the student's error, usually with rising intonation ('My sister have?'). This teacher stops just before the error and waits for the student to complete it.
A recast supplies the correct form. Here the teacher withholds it so the student must produce it.
A clarification request ('Pardon?') signals a breakdown without pinpointing the problem. Pausing right at the error invites the student to complete it correctly.

questions.key: Elicitation = the teacher pauses or asks so the student supplies the correct form (e.g., 'My sister …?').

questions.stimulus:
Grade 8 Integrated ENL/ELA:
Student (Expanding; home language Polish): Last summer my family has visited Ecuador.
Teacher: "Last summer" is a finished time in the past, so we need the simple past here, not the present perfect.
Student: Oh—my family visited Ecuador.
questions.stem: The teacher's response is best classified as which type of corrective feedback?
options: Metalinguistic feedback
Explicit correction
Recast
Repetition
questions.why: Metalinguistic feedback gives comments, information, or questions about the form of the student's utterance without supplying the correct form. Here the teacher explains the rule (a finished past time takes the simple past) and leaves the student to produce visited. Explicit correction would both mark the error and give the correct form ('Not has visited: visited'). Like elicitation, metalinguistic feedback pushes students to repair their own errors.

traps.note: Explicit correction signals the error AND provides the correct form. This teacher explains the rule but leaves the form for the student to produce.
A recast quietly reformulates the sentence correctly, with no grammar talk. This teacher gives grammatical information instead of a model.
Repetition would echo the error with emphasis ('Has visited?'). The teacher instead names the tense that is needed.

questions.key: Metalinguistic feedback = a grammatical comment or clue about the error, without giving the correct form.

questions.stimulus:
Grade 2 science center:
Student (Entering; home language Arabic): Teacher, I need the … the cut thing.
Teacher: Sorry, what do you need?
Student: The scissors! For cut the paper.
questions.stem: The teacher's question "Sorry, what do you need?" is an example of which move?
options: Recast
Confirmation check
Clarification request
Metalinguistic feedback
questions.why: A clarification request ('Pardon?' 'What do you mean?') signals that the listener did not understand and asks the speaker to repeat or reformulate. In Long's Interaction Hypothesis, this kind of negotiation of meaning pushes learners to modify their output, as this student does by producing scissors. A confirmation check would instead offer the listener's interpretation ('The scissors?').

traps.note: A recast supplies a corrected version. This teacher doesn't offer any word; she asks the student to say it again.
A confirmation check offers the listener's interpretation for the speaker to confirm ('The scissors?'). The teacher offers none; she asks what the student needs.
Metalinguistic feedback gives information about language form. The teacher's question is about meaning, not grammar.

questions.key: Clarification request = 'What do you mean?': the listener asks the speaker to repeat or reformulate.

questions.stem: A grade 9 Expanding student often says "more better" even though her teacher has recast the error many times; she shows no sign of noticing the recasts. The teacher wants her to produce the correct form herself. Which feedback is most likely to accomplish this goal?
options: Keep recasting the error ("Yes, it's better") consistently each time it occurs in class.
Write better on her paper and have her copy the correct form ten times for homework.
Prompt her with "Can you say that another way?" and give her time to reformulate it.
Ignore the error, since errors at the Expanding level resolve on their own with more input.
questions.why: Lyster and Ranta found that recasts, though the most common type of feedback, lead to less learner-generated repair than prompts such as elicitation and metalinguistic feedback, which push students to retrieve and produce the correct form themselves. For a persistent error that recasts haven't fixed, a prompt that makes her reformulate is the better choice.

traps.note: Recasts are the most common type of feedback, but they often go unnoticed and lead to less self-repair, as has already happened with this student.
Copying a word in isolation doesn't make her retrieve the form during communication, and it can feel punitive.
Input alone may not fix a persistent error. Without prompts that help her notice the gap, the error risks fossilizing.

questions.key: For self-repair of persistent errors, use prompts (elicitation, metalinguistic feedback) rather than more recasts.

questions.stem: During a whole-class sharing circle, a grade 3 Emerging student excitedly tells about her new baby brother, making several errors in verb tense. What is the most effective teacher response?
options: Stop her after each error and have her repeat the corrected sentence before she goes on.
Ignore the tense errors entirely, since grammar instruction does not help Emerging students.
Suggest that she write the story first so she can check her verbs before she shares aloud.
Respond to her news, recast one key form in passing, and note the pattern for a mini-lesson.
questions.why: In a meaning-focused activity the goal is fluency and communication. The teacher responds to the message, models a correct form unobtrusively with a recast, and records error patterns to teach later in a focused mini-lesson. Interrupting repeatedly raises the affective filter and shifts attention from meaning to form.

traps.note: Interrupting after every error shifts attention from meaning to form and raises her affective filter in front of the class.
Krashen's ideas don't mean that form never matters. Focused instruction on the tense pattern later is helpful; ignoring it entirely misses the chance.
Making accuracy a precondition for sharing turns a fluency activity into an accuracy exercise and puts form ahead of meaning.

questions.key: In meaning-focused talk, respond to the message, recast lightly, and save error patterns for later focused instruction.

questions.stem: Which adjustment to teacher talk is most likely to make a grade 5 science explanation comprehensible to Emerging students?
options: Using a slightly slower rate, shorter sentences, paraphrase, and gestures or visuals for key ideas
Speaking more loudly and repeating each sentence word for word until the students nod
Avoiding academic vocabulary and using everyday words in its place for science concepts
Reading the textbook passage aloud at a normal pace so students hear authentic academic English
questions.why: Comprehensible input depends on speech suited to students' proficiency: a slightly slower rate, clear enunciation, shorter and less complex sentences, pauses, paraphrase and repetition, and gestures and visuals. This is SIOP's Comprehensible Input component. Academic vocabulary stays in the lesson but is made understandable; volume and watered-down content don't help.

traps.note: Volume doesn't create understanding, and nodding isn't evidence of comprehension. Rewording and visuals do the work.
ELLs need academic vocabulary. Make it comprehensible with visuals and paraphrase instead of removing it.
Unmodified reading aloud is authentic, but for Emerging students it isn't comprehensible input; there is no adjustment or support.

questions.key: Comprehensible teacher talk: slower rate, shorter sentences, paraphrase, pauses, gestures and visuals, with academic vocabulary kept.

questions.stem: A grade 7 social studies teacher asks a question and calls on the first student who raises a hand, usually within a second or two. Her ELLs rarely participate. Which change would most likely increase their participation?
options: Ask the ELLs only yes/no questions so that they can respond quickly and successfully.
Extend the wait time and have all students rehearse answers with a partner before calling on anyone.
Call on the ELLs first, before other students have a chance to raise their hands, to hold them accountable.
Have the ELLs write their answers silently while the rest of the class discusses aloud.
questions.why: ELLs need extra processing time to understand a question, form an answer, and find the English to express it. Extending wait time and using structures such as think-pair-share let students rehearse with a partner first. That lowers anxiety and increases both the number and the quality of responses.

traps.note: Limiting ELLs to yes/no questions lowers expectations. They need time and support to answer higher-level questions.
Including ELLs is the right goal, but calling on them instantly gives no processing time and can raise anxiety.
Separating ELLs from the oral discussion removes their chance to practice academic talk.

questions.key: Extend wait time and let students rehearse with a partner (think-pair-share) before calling on anyone.

questions.stem: A grade 4 teacher is introducing the concept of erosion to a class that includes several Emerging students. Which approach would make the concept most comprehensible?
options: Give students a dictionary definition of erosion to copy into their notebooks and memorize
Explain erosion slowly and clearly, offering several synonyms to clarify the term's meaning
Demonstrate with a tray of soil and running water while naming the process, then label photos
Translate the word erosion into each home language and then move on to the next concept
questions.why: Hands-on demonstrations, realia, and visuals make abstract concepts concrete: students see erosion happen while they hear the language that names it, so the input is context-embedded (Cummins). Labeling photos of real erosion afterward connects the model to the world and supports later talk and writing.

traps.note: A copied definition is abstract, decontextualized language. It doesn't show students what erosion is.
