Clear talk helps, but words alone keep the concept abstract and context-reduced. Students need to see it.
A translation can help, but a label doesn't build the concept, especially if students don't know it in their home language either.

questions.key: Make concepts comprehensible with demonstrations, realia, and visuals paired with the language, not words alone.

questions.stem: A teacher divides a grade 8 article on renewable energy into four sections. Each student in a home group reads one section, meets with classmates from other groups who read the same section, and then returns to teach it to the home group. Which cooperative learning structure is this?
options: Think-Pair-Share
Numbered Heads Together
Jigsaw
Inside-Outside Circle
questions.why: In a Jigsaw, each member of a home group becomes an 'expert' on one part of the material in an expert group and then teaches it to the home group. Because every student holds information the others need, Jigsaw builds positive interdependence and individual accountability, and it gives ELLs authentic reasons to speak and listen.

traps.note: Think-Pair-Share has students think alone, discuss with a partner, and share. No one becomes an expert on a separate section.
In Numbered Heads Together, group members discuss a question together, and the teacher calls a number to choose who answers.
Inside-Outside Circle arranges students in two circles that rotate so that each student talks with a series of partners.

questions.key: Jigsaw: home group → expert group on one section → return to teach. It builds interdependence and accountability.

questions.stimulus:
Transcript, grade 10 Integrated ENL/ELA small group (Expanding students):
S1: I think the narrator is brave.
S2: I agree.
S3: Me too.
S1: OK. Next question.
questions.stem: The teacher wants discussions like this one to become more extended and academic. Which instructional step would be most effective?
options: Model and practice moves like elaborating, citing evidence, and building on ideas, with frames and roles.
Replace small-group talk with teacher-led questioning so that the teacher can control the quality of answers.
Give the groups more discussion time, since deeper conversations will develop naturally with practice.
Record the discussions and grade each student's speech for grammatical accuracy to raise expectations.
questions.why: Structured academic talk has to be taught. Students learn conversation moves (elaborate and clarify, support with evidence, paraphrase, build on or challenge ideas) through modeling, frames such as 'Building on what you said…' or 'What in the text makes you think that?', and assigned roles. Adding time rarely changes the pattern, and teacher-led questioning or grammar grading reduces student talk.

traps.note: Teacher-led questioning reduces student talk. ELLs need structured opportunities to talk with peers.
Time helps, but without explicit instruction in conversation moves, the 'I agree / me too' pattern usually continues.
Grading speech for grammar puts form ahead of meaning and discourages risk-taking in discussion.

questions.key: Teach academic conversation moves explicitly: model, frame, and practice elaborating, supporting, and building on ideas.

questions.stimulus:
Grade 5 partner task (giving directions for a plant experiment):
S1 (Transitioning; home language Bengali): Then you put the seeds in the … the small glass.
S2 (Emerging; home language Urdu): The small glass? You mean the jar?
S1: Yes, the jar. Then you add water.
questions.stem: S2's response ("The small glass? You mean the jar?") is best described as which negotiation-of-meaning move?
options: Comprehension check
Clarification request
Elicitation
Confirmation check
questions.why: In Long's Interaction Hypothesis, negotiation of meaning involves three moves. A confirmation check is the listener's attempt to confirm understanding by repeating or rephrasing what was heard, usually with rising intonation ('The small glass? You mean the jar?'). A clarification request asks the speaker to explain ('What do you mean?'), and a comprehension check is the speaker asking whether the listener understood ('Do you know what I mean?').

traps.note: A comprehension check comes from the speaker, checking that the listener understood ('Do you know what I mean?'). S2 is the listener checking her own understanding.
A clarification request asks the speaker to explain ('What do you mean?') without offering an interpretation. S2 offers her guess, the jar, for confirmation.
Elicitation is a teacher feedback move that prompts a student to produce a correct form. S2 is a peer confirming meaning, not prompting a correction.

questions.key: Confirmation check = the listener repeats or rephrases to confirm ('You mean the jar?'); comprehension check = the speaker asks 'Understand?'

questions.stem: A grade 6 ESOL teacher wants an activity that will require her Emerging and Transitioning students to negotiate meaning and push their spoken output, in line with Long's and Swain's research. Which activity best fits this purpose?
options: Think-pair-share on a question about a story, with a sentence frame for students' answers
Choral reading of a dialogue about public transportation, followed by comprehension questions
A video about city transportation, followed by a cloze passage that students complete alone
A two-way information gap in which partners combine halves of a bus map to plan a route
questions.why: In a two-way information gap, each partner holds information the other needs, so communication is required. Breakdowns trigger negotiation of meaning (clarification requests, confirmation checks), which Long links to acquisition, and students must produce comprehensible output, which Swain argues helps them notice gaps. Think-pair-share is valuable interaction, but partners share the same question and information.

traps.note: Think-pair-share is valuable interaction, but partners share the same question and information, so they aren't required to negotiate meaning.
Choral reading produces scripted speech, not the learners' own output, and nothing has to be negotiated.
Watching a video and filling in a cloze alone involves no interaction or spoken output.

questions.key: Two-way information gaps require exchanging unknown information, which maximizes negotiation of meaning and pushed output.

questions.stem: After giving multistep directions for a lab, a grade 7 teacher wants to check whether her Emerging students understood. Which approach gives her the most reliable information?
options: Asking the class, "Does everybody understand?" and watching for students to nod
Having every student point to each step on an illustrated card and retell the steps to a partner
Repeating the directions a second time, more slowly, so that everyone in the room has heard them
Asking the most proficient student to summarize the directions aloud for the class
questions.why: General questions like 'Do you understand?' are unreliable, because students may nod to be polite or may not realize what they missed. Effective comprehension checks require every student to show understanding by pointing, sequencing, demonstrating, or retelling. That gives the teacher real evidence and shows exactly which steps to reteach.

traps.note: Yes/no checks are unreliable: students may nod to be polite or may not realize what they missed.
Repetition can aid comprehension, but it gives the teacher no evidence of who understood.
One strong student's summary says nothing about whether the Emerging students understood; they only listen.

questions.key: Check comprehension by having students show or retell (point, demonstrate, sequence), not by asking 'Do you understand?'

lessons.title: NYS Program Models & Part 154 Service Requirements
lessons.why: Expect items that ask you to name a program model from a description, check a student's weekly ENL schedule against Part 154, and apply the bilingual-program trigger and parent choice.

body.h: The three program options parents choose from
body.md:
Under CR Part 154, every identified ELL is served in one of three program types. Parents learn about all three at an orientation, in their preferred language, before they choose.

- **ENL (English as a New Language):** English language development delivered in English, through **Stand-alone ENL** and **Integrated ENL**. Home languages can and should still be used as supports.
- **Transitional Bilingual Education (TBE):** home language arts, content taught in the home language and in English, and ENL. English instruction increases over time, and the goal is to **transition** students to English-only instruction.
- **Dual Language (DL):** literacy and content in two languages over many years, with the goal of **bilingualism and biliteracy**, academic achievement, and cross-cultural understanding.

Dual Language comes in two forms:

- **One-way:** students come mostly from one language group (for example, Spanish-speaking ELLs and former ELLs).
- **Two-way:** ELLs and English-proficient students learn together, ideally in a balanced mix, each group learning the other's language.

The quick sort: if the home language is phased out, it's TBE. If the home language is kept for biliteracy, it's Dual Language. If English-proficient students are deliberately mixed in, it's two-way. Note that bilingual programs still include ENL: a TBE student gets home language arts, bilingual content, **and** ENL units for her level.

**Stand-alone ENL** is taught by a certified ESOL teacher to ELLs. Its purpose is to build the English students need to succeed in their core content classes. The best Stand-alone lessons are anchored in what students are studying (the vocabulary, sentence patterns, and language functions of this month's science or ELA unit), not a separate grammar track or homework help.

**Integrated ENL** delivers core content and English language development at the same time, in a class with English-proficient peers. It must be taught by either:

- one teacher **dually certified** in the content area and ESOL, or
- a certified content teacher and a certified ESOL teacher **co-teaching**.

A bilingual paraprofessional is a valuable support, and so is a content teacher with plenty of ELL-focused CTLE hours. Neither one counts toward Integrated ENL minutes.

body.h: Units of study, grades K–8 (memorize this)
body.md:
One unit of study is 180 minutes per week. Required minutes go down as proficiency goes up, and the Stand-alone portion shrinks first.

- **Entering:** 360 min = 180 Stand-alone + 180 Integrated ENL/ELA
- **Emerging:** 360 min = 90 Stand-alone + 180 Integrated ENL/ELA + 90 flexible (Stand-alone or Integrated)
- **Transitioning:** 180 min = 90 Integrated ENL/ELA + 90 flexible
- **Expanding:** 180 min of Integrated ENL in ELA **or another core content area**
- **Commanding (former ELL):** 90 min of Integrated ENL or other approved former-ELL services, for 2 years

Patterns worth noticing:

- The totals run 360 → 360 → 180 → 180 → 90.
- Integrated ENL in **ELA** is required for Entering, Emerging, and Transitioning. Only at Expanding may the Integrated minutes be in science, math, or social studies instead.
- From Transitioning on, Stand-alone ENL is no longer required. At Transitioning it can still fill the flexible 90; at Expanding all 180 required minutes are Integrated.

High school Entering students receive more time (540 minutes), but you won't need the 9–12 breakdown.

A student exits ELL status by scoring **Commanding** on the NYSESLAT, or by scoring **Expanding** plus Level 3 or higher on the Grades 3–8 ELA test (or 65 or higher on the Regents ELA exam). Exit is not the end of support. Former ELLs get **90 minutes a week** of Integrated ENL (or other approved former-ELL services) for **two years**, and they keep ELL testing accommodations for two years.

Don't confuse this with ESSA, which lets states keep former ELs in the EL subgroup for up to **four** years for accountability. That is a reporting rule, not a service rule.

body.h: The bilingual trigger and parent choice
body.md:
A district **must** provide a bilingual education program when there are **20 or more ELLs with the same home language in the same grade level, counted districtwide**. All three conditions are required:

- **Same home language:** 24 grade 4 ELLs who speak four different languages don't count.
- **Same grade:** nine Arabic speakers in each of grades 3, 4, and 5 don't count.
- **Districtwide:** 22 Bengali-speaking second graders spread across three schools **do** count, even though no building has 20.

Parents still choose. If parents decline a bilingual program, the student goes into **ENL** with the full units of study for his or her level; declining bilingual is not declining services. When numbers fall below the trigger (say, six Pashto-speaking fifth graders), the student is served in ENL. Teachers can still use the home language through bilingual glossaries, home-language texts, and translanguaging.

body.h: How these items look on the exam
body.md:
Most Part 154 items are applied, not pure recall:

- **Schedule check:** a table of students, levels, and minutes; find the one out of compliance. Check each **component** before the total. A student can have 360 minutes and still fall short if the Integrated time isn't in ELA.
- **Program ID:** a brochure or principal's description. Decide among TBE, one-way DL, two-way DL, and ENL from the goal (transition or biliteracy) and the student mix.
- **Policy response:** a principal's proposal or a parent's request. Choose the response that is both compliant and good for kids.

When two options look right, prefer the one that keeps the ELL in grade-level instruction with qualified teachers and honors the parents' choice.

traps: Exam trap: The total minutes match but a component is wrong. Entering and Emerging students need 180 minutes of Integrated ENL in ELA specifically.
Exam trap: Counting the bilingual trigger per school. It is 20+ ELLs with the same home language in the same grade, districtwide.
Exam trap: Treating a declined bilingual program as declined services. The student is placed in ENL with full units of study.
Exam trap: Calling a one-language-group program TBE when its goal is biliteracy. That is one-way Dual Language.
Exam trap: Counting paraprofessional support, or a content teacher with ELL-focused PD hours, as Integrated ENL.

terms.d: English as a New Language: a program of English language development delivered through Stand-alone and Integrated ENL.
ELL class taught by a certified ESOL teacher to build the English students need for core content success.
Content plus English development, taught by a dually certified teacher or co-taught by certified content and ESOL teachers.
Integrated ENL delivered in the ELA class; required for Entering, Emerging, and Transitioning students in K–8.
Transitional Bilingual Education: home language arts, bilingual content, and ENL; the goal is transition to English-only instruction.
Two-language program serving mainly one language group, aiming for bilingualism and biliteracy.
Two-language program combining ELLs and English-proficient students, aiming for biliteracy for all.
180 minutes of instruction per week.
Emerging and Transitioning minutes that may be delivered as either Stand-alone or Integrated ENL.
20+ ELLs with the same home language in the same grade, districtwide: the district must provide a bilingual program.
90 minutes a week of Integrated ENL or approved services for 2 years after exit, plus testing accommodations.
Session where parents learn about TBE, Dual Language, and ENL in their preferred language before choosing.
Literacy instruction in the home language; a core component of bilingual programs.
NYS Commissioner's Regulations governing ELL identification, program options, units of study, and services.

lessons.tip: On schedule questions, check each required component (Stand-alone, Integrated ENL/ELA, flexible) before you look at the total.

lessons.title: Approaches & Methods: Recognize Them, Evaluate Them
lessons.why: The exam describes a classroom or a transcript and asks which method it reflects, what theory underlies it, or which approach best fits a goal.

body.h: Read the fingerprint, not the label
body.md:
Method items give you a short vignette and four method names. Each method has one or two **fingerprint** features. Find them, and ignore surface details such as objects on a desk, a moment of translation, or an audio recorder.

Ask three questions:

- **What does the teacher do?** Talk constantly, stay silent, translate, drill, counsel, or design tasks?
- **What do the students do?** Move, repeat, answer in full sentences, dictate, complete a task, or apply a strategy?
- **What is the goal?** Accurate habits, comprehension first, communication, content learning, or strategic learning?

- **Grammar-Translation:** translate written texts, memorize bilingual word lists, and learn rules **deductively** (rule first, then practice). It builds knowledge *about* English but little oral communication, which is its big limitation for ELLs.
- **Direct Method:** English only, never translate. Meaning comes through demonstration, realia, and pictures in **question-and-answer** exchanges. Grammar is learned **inductively**, and full-sentence answers and good pronunciation are expected.
- **Audiolingual Method (ALM):** memorized dialogues and **pattern drills** (substitution, repetition, chain), immediate correction, and praise as reinforcement. It is rooted in **Skinner's behaviorism** and structural linguistics: language as habit formation.

Direct Method vs. ALM is a favorite trap, because both are oral and English-only. Q&A about objects points to the Direct Method; drilling a pattern and rewarding the correct response points to ALM.

A typical ALM drill: T: "I am going to the store. She." Ss: "She is going to the store." T: "Good! They."

- **Total Physical Response (TPR, Asher):** the teacher gives commands and students respond with actions; speech is not forced. It is excellent for Entering students and young learners but limited for abstract language.
- **Natural Approach (Krashen & Terrell):** abundant comprehensible input, a silent (preproduction) period, questions matched to the stage (yes/no and either/or, then open-ended), and no correction of errors in early stages, to keep the affective filter low.
- **Silent Way (Gattegno):** the teacher is mostly silent and uses Cuisenaire rods and color-coded sound charts; students discover rules and self-correct.
- **Suggestopedia (Lozanov):** a relaxed setting, comfortable chairs, baroque music, long dialogues, and positive suggestion to remove mental barriers.
- **Community Language Learning (Curran):** students sit in a circle and say what they want in the home language. The teacher-counselor (the "knower") gives the English, students repeat it, the talk is recorded and transcribed, and students reflect on their feelings.

TPR vs. the Natural Approach: both delay speech, but commands answered with actions is TPR. The Natural Approach is a broader input-based approach that may *include* TPR activities.

- **Communicative Language Teaching (CLT):** grounded in Hymes's communicative competence. It features real purposes, information exchange, negotiation of meaning, fluency and appropriateness, and grammar taught in service of communication. It is an umbrella approach.
- **Task-Based Language Teaching (TBLT):** units built around a task with a real, non-linguistic **outcome** (an itinerary, a decision, a product), often in a cycle of pre-task, task, report, and language focus. It is a specific, strong form of CLT, so if the stem says "most specifically," choose TBLT.
- **Content-Based Instruction (CBI):** English is learned through academic subject matter, so language and content develop together. Sheltered instruction, SIOP, and CALLA all build on it.
- **Language Experience Approach (LEA):** students share an experience and dictate an account, the teacher writes it, and the text becomes their reading material. It is ideal for beginning readers and for SIFE of any age.

body.h: Sheltered and strategy models: SIOP and CALLA
body.md:
**SIOP (Echevarría, Vogt & Short)** has **8 components** and 30 features: Lesson Preparation, Building Background, Comprehensible Input, Strategies, Interaction, Practice & Application, Lesson Delivery, and Review & Assessment. Know what goes where:

- **Building Background:** link to students' experiences, link past learning to new learning, and emphasize key vocabulary.
- **Comprehensible Input:** speech suited to proficiency, clear explanation of tasks, modeling, visuals, and gestures.
- **Lesson Preparation:** content and language objectives, adapted materials, and meaningful activities.

**CALLA (Chamot & O'Malley)** integrates grade-level content, academic language, and **explicit learning-strategy instruction** (metacognitive, cognitive, social/affective) in five phases: **preparation, presentation, practice, self-evaluation, expansion**. A teacher who names a strategy, models it, has students practice it, and then asks whether it helped is doing CALLA.

Translanguaging (Ofelia García; CUNY-NYSIEB) treats a bilingual student's languages as **one integrated repertoire** and plans for students to use all of it to learn. Students might discuss in same-language pairs, take notes in any language, and read related home-language texts, then produce in English or in more than one language.

Key points for the exam:

- It is **planned**, not a last-resort crutch.
- Teachers do **not** need to speak every home language; they design the structures.
- It complements grade-level English texts and tasks rather than replacing them.

Some items ask which method best fits a goal or what a method's limitation is. Match the method to the need:

- Newcomers who need low-anxiety listening: TPR, the Natural Approach.
- Beginning readers, including older SIFE: LEA.
- Academic content together with language: CBI, SIOP, CALLA.
- Authentic communication: CLT, TBLT.

Methods that put form before meaning (ALM, Grammar-Translation) are rarely the best answer for building ELLs' communicative and academic English, although a short drill or some explicit grammar can play a small role inside a meaningful lesson.

traps: Exam trap: Direct Method vs. Audiolingual. Both are oral and English-only; Q&A with objects and inductive grammar = Direct Method, while pattern drills with reinforcement = ALM.
Exam trap: TPR vs. Natural Approach. Commands answered with actions = TPR; stage-matched questions and abundant input = Natural Approach.
Exam trap: Choosing CLT when the stem asks for the most specific approach for a unit built on a task with a real outcome (TBLT).
Exam trap: Calling any lesson that teaches a strategy SIOP. The five-phase explicit strategy cycle is CALLA.
Exam trap: Assuming translanguaging requires the teacher to speak every home language.

terms.d: Deductive rule learning, translation of written texts, and vocabulary lists; little oral communication.
Target language only; Q&A with objects and pictures; inductive grammar; full-sentence, accurate answers.
Dialogue memorization and pattern drills with reinforcement; based on behaviorism and structural linguistics.
Asher: students respond to commands with physical actions before being asked to speak.
Krashen & Terrell: comprehensible input, a silent period, stage-matched questions, low affective filter.
Gattegno: mostly silent teacher, Cuisenaire rods, color-coded charts, discovery, and self-correction.
Lozanov: relaxed setting, music, long dialogues, and positive suggestion to lower barriers to learning.
Curran: teacher-counselor translates learners' messages; talk is recorded, transcribed, and reflected on.
Communicative Language Teaching: real communication, negotiation of meaning, fluency and appropriateness.
Task-Based Language Teaching: instruction built around tasks with real outcomes, followed by a language focus.
Content-Based Instruction: English learned through grade-level academic content.
Students dictate an account of a shared experience; the teacher-written text becomes their reading material.
Sheltered instruction model with 8 components and 30 features for planning, teaching, and observing.
Chamot & O'Malley: content, academic language, and explicit strategy instruction in five phases.
García: planned use of students' full linguistic repertoire as a resource for learning.

lessons.tip: Find the single fingerprint feature (commands, silence, drills, task outcome, dictated text, strategy cycle) and match it; ignore surface details.

lessons.title: Planning: Objectives, Language Demands & Scaffolding by Level
lessons.why: Planning items ask you to pick the best language objective, analyze a task's language demands, match scaffolds to a proficiency level, or fix a lesson sequence.

body.md:
A **content objective** states what students will learn about the subject: *Students will describe the four stages of a butterfly's life cycle.*

A **language objective** states how students will use language to learn and show that content. A strong one names:

- the **function** (the purpose: describe, sequence, compare, explain, argue),
- the **domain** (listening, speaking, reading, writing), and
- the supporting **forms** (structures and vocabulary).

Example: *Students will orally sequence the life-cycle stages using first, next, then, and finally.*

Watch for imposters on the exam:

- An **activity** ("complete a picture sort") is not an objective.
- A restated **content goal** ("learn the stages") is not a language objective.
- An **isolated skill** ("spell four words on a quiz") is language-related but disconnected from the lesson's real language demand.

Language objectives sit **alongside** grade-level content objectives. They make the lesson's language visible so it gets taught and assessed; they don't replace content goals with easier ones.

Before teaching, look at what the text or task demands at three levels:

- **Word/phrase:** Tier 2 and Tier 3 vocabulary, idioms (*kept in check*), multiple-meaning words.
- **Sentence:** complex structures such as embedded clauses, passive voice, nominalization, and participial phrases (*…grew rapidly, resulting in overgrazing*).
- **Discourse:** how a whole text or response is organized, such as an argument (claim → evidence → reasoning), an explanation, or a narrative.

The task matters as much as the text. "Were the colonists justified? Support your claim with evidence from Documents A and B" is an **argue** task. Students need claim language, citation language (*According to Document A…*), and connectors (*because, therefore*). Vocabulary and readability are part of the demand, but they are rarely the most complete analysis.

For dense sentences, unpack them into short sentences, then repack them, so students learn to read and eventually write such sentences.

The NYS New Language Arts Progressions show the same grade-level standard at all five levels, with support decreasing from Entering (substantial) to Commanding (independent). The task stays the same while the support changes:

- **Entering:** visuals, realia, labeled diagrams, home-language resources and bilingual glossaries, partner work, words and short phrases, simple frames (*It has __ sides.*).
- **Emerging:** word banks, sentence frames, partly completed graphic organizers, models.
- **Transitioning:** sentence starters, organizers, more open tasks, peer support.
- **Expanding:** targeted support for complex sentences, transitions, and precise vocabulary; feedback on cohesion.
- **Commanding:** largely independent, with occasional support for advanced academic language.

**Amplify, don't simplify** (Walqui). Keep the grade-level text and add temporary supports: chunking, pre-teaching key concepts, glosses, visuals, and guiding questions. A simplified summary or a lower-grade text lowers rigor and strips out the language students need to learn.

Gradual release of responsibility moves through four stages:

- **I do:** the teacher models and thinks aloud.
- **We do:** guided, shared practice (for example, a summary written together).
- **You do together:** collaborative practice with peers.
- **You do alone:** independent work.

Two exam patterns:

- **Missing stages:** a plan that jumps from modeling straight to independent work needs guided and collaborative practice added, not just more modeling.
- **Recursive release:** when formative evidence shows that a few students aren't ready, pull them into a brief guided group while the others continue. Don't reteach everyone, and don't drop the hard part of the task.

Scaffolds are **temporary**. A frame used unchanged from September to January caps growth, so fade it to open starters and connector banks, then to independence.

Backward design (Wiggins & McTighe) plans in three stages:

- **Identify desired results:** the standards-based content and language goals.
- **Determine acceptable evidence:** how students will show they met the goals.
- **Plan learning experiences:** activities, materials, and scaffolds.

For ELLs, the key idea is alignment: the assessment must match the objective's domain, function, and forms. If the language objective is *orally explain the causes of the seasons using because and as a result*, the evidence is an oral explanation checked against those criteria. A multiple-choice quiz or a paragraph graded for spelling measures something else.

When choosing among plans, prefer the one that:

- keeps **grade-level content and standards** for every student,
- matches **support to the stated proficiency level** instead of one-size-fits-all,
- gets students **using language** (speaking and writing), not just copying or listening, and
- includes a clear path to **independence**.

Wrong answers usually water down the content, pull the student out of the content class, give everyone identical supports, or demand unsupported work beyond the student's level.

traps: Exam trap: Choosing an activity or a restated content goal as the 'language objective.'
Exam trap: Treating vocabulary as the whole language demand; argument and explanation tasks also carry sentence- and discourse-level demands.
Exam trap: Simplifying or swapping the text for Emerging students instead of scaffolding the grade-level text.
Exam trap: Adding more modeling when the plan is missing guided and collaborative practice.
Exam trap: Keeping the same scaffold all year; scaffolds should fade as proficiency grows.

How students will use language (function, domain, forms) to learn and show the content.
The purpose of language use: describe, sequence, compare, explain, argue.
The grammatical structures and vocabulary used to carry out a function.
Listening, speaking, reading, or writing.
The word-, sentence-, and discourse-level language a text or task requires.
Temporary, planned support that lets students do grade-level work they can't yet do alone.
Walqui: keep complex grade-level text and add supports rather than watering it down.
I do → we do → you do together → you do alone.
Wiggins & McTighe: desired results → acceptable evidence → learning activities.

lessons.title: Comprehensible Input, Interaction & Corrective Feedback
lessons.why: Expect transcripts that ask you to name a feedback type or negotiation move, plus scenarios on making input comprehensible, increasing participation, and structuring talk.

body.md:
Krashen's i+1 is input slightly beyond students' current level, made understandable through context. In class that looks like:

- **Teacher talk:** a slightly slower rate, clear enunciation, shorter sentences, pauses, paraphrase and repetition, and fewer idioms. Keep academic vocabulary and make it understandable rather than removing it. Volume doesn't help.
- **Visuals, realia, demonstrations:** show erosion with a tray of soil and running water while naming it, then label photos. This makes the language **context-embedded** (Cummins).
- **Gestures and modeling:** act it out, point, show a finished example.

**Comprehension checks** must produce evidence. "Does everybody understand?" invites polite nods. Instead, have every student point to the step on an illustrated card, demonstrate, sequence, or retell to a partner.

ELLs have to understand the question, form an answer, and find the English to say it, and all of that takes time. When a teacher calls on the first raised hand within a second or two, ELLs drop out.

Better moves:

- **Extend wait time** (several seconds or more) after asking a question.
- Use **think-pair-share:** think alone, rehearse with a partner, then share.
- Let students **rehearse** with frames or in the home language before speaking to the whole class.

Avoid fixes that lower rigor (only yes/no questions for ELLs) or exclude ELLs (they write silently while others talk).

**Long's Interaction Hypothesis:** when communication breaks down, learners **negotiate meaning**, and those adjustments make input comprehensible and drive acquisition. The three moves:

- **Clarification request:** "Sorry, what do you need?" The listener asks the speaker to explain.
- **Confirmation check:** "The small glass? You mean the jar?" The listener offers an interpretation to confirm.
- **Comprehension check:** "Do you know what I mean?" The speaker checks the listener.

**Swain's Output Hypothesis:** producing language makes learners notice gaps, test hypotheses, and reflect on form.

The activity that maximizes both is a **two-way information gap**: each partner holds information the other needs (two halves of a bus map), so they must exchange and negotiate. Think-pair-share is good interaction, but partners share the same information.

Cooperative structures to know:

- **Jigsaw:** home group → expert group on one section → return to teach it.
- **Numbered Heads Together:** the group discusses; the teacher calls a number to choose who answers.
- **Inside-Outside Circle:** two circles rotate so students talk with a series of partners.
- **Think-Pair-Share:** think, pair, share.

"I agree." "Me too." "Next question." Unstructured group talk often stays shallow, so academic conversation has to be taught:

- Model **conversation moves**: elaborate and clarify, support with text evidence, paraphrase, build on or challenge an idea.
- Provide **frames**: *Building on what ___ said…*, *What in the text makes you think that?*, *I see it differently because…*
- Assign **roles** (questioner, evidence finder, summarizer) and use a protocol.

More time alone rarely changes the pattern, and replacing peer talk with teacher-led Q&A reduces student output.

body.h: The six corrective feedback types (Lyster & Ranta)
body.md:
Student: *Yesterday I go to the library.*

- **Explicit correction:** "Not *go*. Say *went*." Signals the error and gives the form.
- **Recast:** "Oh, you *went* to the library yesterday?" Reformulates correctly with no signal of error. It is the most common type; it is unobtrusive but often goes unnoticed.
- **Clarification request:** "Sorry?" or "What do you mean?"
- **Metalinguistic feedback:** "*Yesterday* is a finished time, so we need the past tense." Gives grammatical information but not the form.
- **Elicitation:** "Yesterday I…?" (pause), "How do we say that?", or "Can you say that another way?" The student supplies the form.
- **Repetition:** "I *GO*?" Repeats the error, usually with rising intonation.

Two distinctions decide most items:

- Explicit correction vs. metalinguistic feedback: **was the correct form given?** If yes, it's explicit correction.
- Elicitation vs. repetition: **did the teacher repeat the error?** If yes, it's repetition. If she stopped before the error or asked for the form, it's elicitation.

- **Meaning-focused activity** (a sharing circle, a discussion): respond to the message first, recast lightly, and **note error patterns** for a later mini-lesson. Constant interruption raises the affective filter.
- **Form-focused moment or persistent error** (*more better* after many recasts): use **prompts** such as elicitation and metalinguistic feedback. Lyster and Ranta found that prompts lead to more **learner-generated repair** than recasts.
- **Level matters:** Entering students need low-anxiety feedback focused on meaning; Expanding students can handle, and benefit from, prompts that push accuracy.

Ignoring every error is not the answer either. Without noticing (Schmidt), persistent errors can fossilize.

traps: Exam trap: Calling any teacher reformulation 'explicit correction.' If there is no signal of error, it is a recast.
Exam trap: Mixing up metalinguistic feedback (rule or clue, no form given) with explicit correction (form given).
Exam trap: Confusing confirmation checks (the listener offers an interpretation) with clarification requests and comprehension checks.
Exam trap: Choosing more recasts when the goal is self-repair; prompts (elicitation, metalinguistic feedback) work better.
Exam trap: Interrupting a meaning-focused activity to correct every error.

terms.d: Krashen: input slightly beyond the learner's level (i+1), made understandable through context and support.
Adjusted teacher speech: slower rate, shorter sentences, paraphrase, pauses, gestures.
Real objects used to make language and concepts concrete.
Pause after a question that gives students time to process and formulate an answer.
A speaker's check that the listener understood; in teaching, a task that makes students show understanding.
Long: interactional adjustments (clarifying, confirming, checking) when communication breaks down.
'What do you mean?' The listener asks the speaker to repeat or reformulate.
'You mean the jar?' The listener repeats or rephrases to confirm understanding.
Task in which each partner holds information the other needs, forcing real exchange.
Students master one section in expert groups, then teach it to their home group.
Feedback that signals the error and provides the correct form.
Implicit correct reformulation of the student's utterance, with no signal that an error occurred.
Comments or questions about the form of an utterance, without giving the correct form.
Prompting the student to supply the correct form: a pause, a question, or a request to reformulate.
Teacher repeats the student's error, usually with rising intonation, to highlight it.
The student's immediate response to feedback, ideally a repair of the error.

lessons.tip: For feedback transcripts, ask: Did the teacher give the correct form? Did she signal an error? Did she repeat the error? Those answers identify the type.
